The Most Dangerous Assumption In AI Security Is That Deployment Means Readiness

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lee Rossey is CTO of SimSpace, advancing AI proving grounds to help orgs prove cyber readiness.
  • It has been revealed that ​There’s a fight going on inside most organizations right now.
  • Security tends to get cast as the blocker, the people who ask awkward questions about risk or about what happens when an agent hallucinates during a critical incident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lee Rossey is CTO of SimSpace, advancing AI proving grounds to help orgs prove cyber readiness.

It has been revealed that ​There’s a fight going on inside most organizations right now. On one side are the people pushing to adopt AI at any cost, often without a clear idea of what they’re adopting. On the other are the people who have to make it work.

Security tends to get cast as the blocker, the people who ask awkward questions about risk or about what happens when an agent hallucinates during a critical incident. But many security people want AI. In security operations, it can take over the tedious work that burns analysts out. It can triage alerts, investigate incidents, summarize cases in plain language and isolate a host at a speed and volume no human team can match.

In a recent development, and we need that speed. Attackers don’t have to sit through governance reviews, and the fear of breaking things doesn’t hold them back when that’s their main aim. Reconnaissance that used to take a human hours now takes an agent minutes, and an agent never gets bored or tired of probing for a way in.

So yes, enterprises need AI in security operations. Nobody serious disputes that. But we can’t just drop agents into the SOC and expect them to perform. How do we know they’ll hold up against an attack they’ve never seen?

Here’s a familiar scenario: A regional bank buys an agentic tool to investigate indicators of compromise, which behaves perfectly in the vendor demo. It takes a known ransomware hash, queries the EDR, pivots into DNS logs, isolates the beaconing host and writes a clean case summary in under two minutes. Sold.

According to recent reports, then it goes into production, and the quirks start to show: A lender the bank recently acquired still logs in local time, so the agent stitches a timeline together five hours out of order. A legacy proxy it was never given access to returns nothing, so the agent reports “no indicators found” instead of the real answer: “I couldn’t look.” The summaries read well and the tickets close, so nothing prompts anyone to look twice, even though the risk is still there.

Now introduce a threat group that highlights up with a tactic the tool has never met. The attackers call the help desk, talk their way into an MFA reset on a finance admin’s account and move through approved remote management tools into the cloud tenant. An indicator-driven agent either closes the alert as benign or maps the behavior to the nearest known group and isolates a host while the attacker keeps working through identity. And if the phishing email claims the activity is an authorized red team exercise, the agent may simply believe it.

The quirks don’t show up in the demo, because a demo only shows an agent doing the tasks it was built for, in an environment set up to cooperate. A real production environment has a complex tech stack, messy data and a threat nobody has seen before. It’s no surprise that agents that look perfect in a controlled evaluation fall apart when the environment is unfamiliar or the information incomplete, and they fall apart faster when someone is deliberately trying to trick them.

Recent findings suggest that security teams need to find the balance between measuring whether an AI system can complete a task and proving it can make the right decisions under pressure. They have to find out how an agent will handle a different environment and the most likely attack scenarios before it goes into production.

It has been revealed that the environment needs to behave like the real thing to be taken seriously, with realistic operating systems and hardware running real applications and real agents on real data. The user side needs real activity, too: people sending emails and working in business applications while admins manage the domain and change network configuration. Every event leaves a trace, so genuine machine and network logs are crucial, too. The agent has to find the real threat in the same noise that analysts wade through every day, and legitimate business activity has to be present to see whether the agent disrupts work it shouldn’t.

Industry observers note that security leaders should start by agreeing on success criteria before testing begins. Decide what counts as a pass and what counts as a fail, and include the cases that should stop a deployment outright, like unauthorized actions or missed escalations. Then set a baseline by running existing analysts and tools through the same scenarios to have something concrete to compare the agent against.

It has been revealed that next, run real attacks against the agent, emulating the tactics and techniques of actual cyber criminal groups. Because the team controls the attack, they know exactly what happened, which means it can be held up against what the agent reported and see where it got things wrong.

Score outcomes over activity, since an agent that closes a lot of tickets or finishes investigations promptly can still leave threats unresolved or need expensive human review to clean up after it. Finally, don’t treat testing as a one-time gate at deployment. Models get updated, attacker techniques shift and data changes, so an agent that performed well in month one may behave differently in month four. Rerun the same attacks against the same environment on a regular schedule to catch that drift early.

Industry observers note that security teams don’t have to be a blocker. Run agents through realistic tests, score what they actually accomplish and retest as things change, meaning teams have evidence instead of opinion. That evidence lets teams tell the business which agents are ready for more autonomy, which need limits and which aren’t ready at all.

Companies that do this will get more out of AI than the ones that skip it, because they’ll know where it can be trusted and where a person still needs to be in the loop. The question from the start still stands: How do we know an agent will hold up against an attack it has never seen? Now we can answer it.​.

Tech Report: What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car.
  • The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:.
  • Sources indicate that A visual exterior inspection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:.

Sources indicate that A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

Sources indicate that A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic challenges that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

In a recent development, reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

It has been revealed that the good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Recent findings suggest that some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

In a recent development, reddit is an online forum where owners share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit owners are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Sources indicate that car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several owners suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

EPS was $1.43, above the high end of our guidance and up 131%. GAAP EPS was $1.26. We delivered free cash flow of $1.9 billion, driven by strong operating profit. Now let's turn to our segment results. Q4 Networking revenue was $3.1 billion, up 12%, consistent with our outlook. Networking orders grew 56% with strong momentum across most product categories. To address this order growth, we increased our networking purchase commitments sequentially by over 25%.

Industry observers note that networking operating profit came in at $675 million, up 6% both year-over-year and sequentially, with operating margins of 22.1%. Campus & Branch revenue grew 17% due to the strength of our self-driving network. Data Center Networking grew 12% and Routing grew 10%, both driven by momentum in cloud demand and partially constrained by supply. Security was down low single digits. Enterprise revenue grew 16% and Service Provider grew 5%. Moving to Cloud & AI. We delivered revenue of $11.3 billion, up 69%. Order growth was up 107%, driving backlog to an all-time high. Operating profit came in at $2.1 billion, up 235% year-over-year and 35% sequentially.

Operating margin was higher than we anticipated, landing at 18.4%, supported by strong favorable pricing dynamics and disciplined cost management. Server revenue grew 95% year-over-year, accelerating sequentially due to ASP growth in traditional servers that offset supply-constrained unit volumes. We delivered triple-digit revenue growth in AI systems and strong double-digit growth in traditional servers and storage. Server orders were up triple digits year-over-year, with strength across key customer segments and major geographies. Storage revenue increased 34%, driven by several large deals in public and enterprise sectors. PCAI orders increased by strong double digits in Q4 as we delivered our largest revenue quarter.

Alletra MP revenue also increased by strong double digits year-over-year and now exceeds an annual run rate of $1 billion, reflecting continued healthy enterprise demand. Total company ARR exceeded $3.5 billion, up 12% as we drove solid growth in our software, services and subscription businesses. Finally, Financial Services revenue was roughly flat year-over-year, reporting record quarterly financing volume of $2.1 billion, up 43% and generated a return on equity exceeding 25%. Based on our continued order momentum and a strong pipeline that is multiples of our backlog, we entered fiscal '27 confident in the durability of the demand environment. Moving to AI-specific demand.

Recent findings suggest that networks for AI demand accelerated in Q4, with orders reaching a record $1.2 billion, up strong triple digits. Within Networking, order growth remained strong in Q4, with Data Center Networking up double digits and Routing up triple digits, driven by large AI data center fabric and data center interconnect demand. We expect Helios and Oracle contributions to drive continued growth as we progress through fiscal '27. For the full year, networks for AI orders grew nearly 200%, with backlog ending the year at $1.7 billion. We have significantly increased our networking purchase commitments and expect to improve order conversion as we progress through fiscal 2027.

In Q4, AI systems orders reached $4.5 billion, up over 130%, with revenue up triple digits to $2.5 billion. Full year AI system orders grew over 45%, with AI systems backlog up nearly 90%, while revenue of $5.8 billion was up 28%. We remain focused on the enterprise and sovereign customer segments, which constitute over 60% of our cumulative AI orders over the past 4 years. We continue to approach large AI server deals with discipline, prioritizing profitability and free cash flow over volume. Turning to transformation. We exited fiscal '26 running ahead of strategy on both our Catalyst initiatives and Juniper integration synergies, which were meaningful contributors to our improved profitability and margin expansion.

In addition, we delivered strong free cash flow this year while absorbing approximately $335 million in Catalyst and Juniper integration costs. Together, Catalyst and Juniper are now expected to deliver approximately $1.2 billion in annual gross run rate savings by the end of fiscal '28. These savings are benefiting both cost of sales and operating expenses while funding investments that drive long-term profitable growth. We see meaningful opportunities ahead to drive additional efficiencies, further optimize our cost structure and strengthen margins across the business. Moving to cash. Q4 operating cash flow was $2.3 billion, and free cash flow totaled $1.9 billion. For the full year, we delivered free cash flow of $4.5 billion.

According to recent reports, our cash conversion cycle improved by 12 days from Q3, driven primarily by a decrease in days inventory due to strong shipment volume and a decrease in days receivable due to more favorable mix of customer billings volume. DPO also improved due to higher purchases to secure strategic component supply and fulfill backlog. Inventory ended the quarter at $14.1 billion, up year-over-year and sequentially, reflecting higher commodity costs, purchases to support customer orders and strategic buys. Cash and cash equivalents ended the year at $5.8 billion, flat versus last year. We used cash on hand to retire $1.25 billion of notes, ending the year with a net leverage ratio of 1.4x, well below our 2x target.

Sources indicate that in fiscal year '26, we returned $2 billion to common shareholders, including $0.8 billion in common dividends. Share repurchases exceeded $1.2 billion with $790 million in Q4. We remain committed to targeting at least 75% of our free cash flow to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases over time. For fiscal year '27, we are targeting approximately $3 billion of share buybacks. Earlier today, we announced that we are raising our quarterly dividend by 19% to $0.17 per share beginning in Q1 '27. Turning to guidance. For Q1, we expect revenue between $14 billion to $14.6 billion. We expect Networking revenue to grow 11% to 13%, with growth accelerating as the year progresses.

It has been revealed that we expect Networking operating margin to improve sequentially to the low to mid-20% range, driven by top line growth and Juniper synergies. In Cloud & AI, we expect revenue to grow 68% to 78%, reflecting sustained demand, higher ASPs in traditional servers and greater AI revenue conversion. We expect operating margin to moderate sequentially to the 16% to 17% range. We expect the sequential decrease in Q1 total operating expense to be in the low 20% range due to lower variable compensation expense, higher Catalyst transformation efficiencies and Juniper synergies capture. We expect operating profit of $2.2 billion to $2.4 billion, with our operating margin rate declining sequentially, driven primarily by higher input costs, partially offset by pricing.

It has been revealed that as a result, we expect EPS between $1.30 and $1.40, and GAAP EPS between $0.88 and $0.98. Turning to our fiscal year '27 outlook. Our updated outlook reflects an expanding pipeline, strong momentum exiting Q4 and increased supply availability driving improved backlog conversion. Our outlook includes expected contribution from Helios. We now expect consolidated revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with approximately 46% of revenue in the first half and 54% in the second half. Networking revenue growth in the high teens to low 20% range, reflecting a more back-end loaded year given the timing of Helios shipments and the anticipated contribution from the Oracle agreement. Networking for AI cumulative orders of $7.5 billion to $8 billion exiting the year.

It has been revealed that cloud & AI revenue growth of 30% to 40%. Company operating profit growth of 23% to 30%. Company operating margin of 14% to 15%. Network operating margin in the mid- to high 20% range. Cloud & AI operating margin of approximately 14%. EPS of $5.05 to $5.35, implying growth of 27% to 35%, with earnings modestly weighted to the second half of the year and free cash flow of at least $5.5 billion. These estimates reflect a fully diluted share count of 1.43 billion, non-GAAP tax rate of 13% and OI&E of approximately $380 million. We expect GAAP EPS of $3.68 to $3.98.

Seasonality will be more muted given backlog, though we do expect Networking growth to accelerate and profitability to improve as the year progresses. We expect gross margin rate to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes increase, including the ramp of Helios. That reflects both the higher mix of AI servers and costs increasing faster than pricing. Importantly, the higher volumes still drive meaningful revenue growth, and we expect gross profit dollars to increase despite the lower gross margin rate. In closing, Q4 capped off an outstanding year for HPE. We generated record financial results, exceeded our fiscal '26 commitments, grew revenue and profitability sequentially throughout the year and improved our operating leverage.

We are entering fiscal '27 with strong momentum and remain focused on executing our strategy, delivering revenue, EPS and free cash flow growth and returning at least 75% of our free cash flow to shareholders. With that, I'll turn the call back to the operator to begin Q&A.

Our team has done a fantastic job integrating Juniper, driving significant growth, expanding profit and position us for what comes next. And we are entering 2027 with an accelerated momentum. We see very strong demand. We believe that demand is durable.

Industry observers note that and what we have guided is a reflection of that momentum and the ability to fulfill for our customers based on the line of sight on the demand backlog and supply availability, which is normally what we do. And obviously, the only sad news about all of this was the loss of our dear friend, Ray Lane, which we will celebrate as a company, but for many years to come because he was a dear friend of mine and an amazing human being. So with that, if I don't speak to you, I wish you a happy Thanksgiving and a great holiday season. I'm sure we're going to talk offline between now and then.

So thank you very much for your time.

Savio scores on debut as Spurs cruise past Charlton in Carabao Cup

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.
  • Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.
  • But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

Industry observers note that “A perfect day for him,” mentioned De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

Industry observers note that “We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”.

In a recent development, "What an introduction!"Sávio scores a brilliant goal on his Spurs debut! 👏 pic.twitter.com/WgmcfgeNpX.

Having watched some of Tottenham’s signings fall to a 3-0 Premier League defeat by Brentford a few days earlier, Sávio’s late impact was the perfect lift for the Spurs supporters.

The club have committed to spending almost £400m this summer, leading to debate by outsiders over whether it will prove to be money well spent and huge waves of excitement within the fanbase.

A deal that could be worth as much as £85m, if add-ons are achieved, for Sávio certainly raised some eyebrows, but the Brazilian provided the perfect response by scoring just 11 minutes into his debut as a late substitute.

According to recent reports, in the 82nd minute, Sávio cut in from the flank and scored with a shot past Charlton goalkeeper Tiernan Brooks. He and the Spurs crowd thought he had a second a few minutes later, but his shot hit Ben Davies on its way into the net and the defender was credited with the goal.

Having sung for Moore earlier in the game, the Spurs fans wasted no time in trying out their new song for Sávio, inspired by the Spandau Ballet hit Gold.

Moore has been expected to move to Cologne on loan, but provided a reminder of his talent by opening the scoring in the first half with only his second goal for the club.

What a hit from Mikey Moore! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/OgSM4qhiqs.

“We have to understand the best solution,” De Zerbi said. “I would like to keep him. He’s young but a good player, but we can’t make the wrong decision. He needs to play, he needs to get games inside him.”.

In a recent development, cutting in from the right, where Sávio is primed to play, Moore surged past his marker and shot from just inside the box. Brooks should have stopped it, but the ball flew past him and into the net.

Three minutes after Moore’s opener, Dominic Solanke scored his first goal since March to offer a reminder of what he can still give De Zerbi, who is poised to welcome Omar Marmoush to Tottenham.

In a recent development, buoyed by his first-half goal, Moore skipped his way around a couple of tackles at the start of the second period but his low cross was cut out. The Spurs fans responded by singing “he’s one of our own.”.

Substitute Kevin Danso netted with his first touch from a header, before Sávio was introduced to steal the show, despite a late consolation goal from Charlton’s Lloyd Jones.

Kevin Danso scores with his first touch since coming on! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/oqUU7wjoJW.

Recent findings suggest that the victory set up a tough third-round trip to Anfield to face Liverpool for Tottenham, but De Zerbi stated: “It’s a great game. If we want to win the competition we have to win the games.

“Sometimes in this competition, it can happen that you play against substantial teams. It’s a great challenge for the players, for me, for our clubs. We have to arrive ready to play in our style, with personality, ready to play a game following the work we are doing on the training ground.”.

Recent findings suggest that A place in the League Cup third round is at stake as Tottenham host Charlton in a London derby at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The last competitive meeting between these sides came in the FA Cup back in January 2011, with Tottenham winning that game 3-0 at White Hart Lane. A then 19-year-old Andros Townsend made his debut that day and scored, with Jermain Defoe scoring a brace.

Sources indicate that tottenham’s Premier League campaign got off to the worst possible start as they lost 3-0 at Brentford last weekend. Tottenham have been very busy during this summer transfer window and that has continued this week. Savio (formerly Savinho) has arrived from Manchester City in a deal that could be worth £85m and the Brazilian could make his Tottenham debut tonight, having been registered in time.

In a recent development, “I think in attacking positions we need players capable one-on one, to create something, to create a chance to score,” Roberto De Zerbi remarked. “In terms of one-on-one, he [Savio] is one of the best players, especially since 2024. He can play on the right side, on the left side. I have known him from a long time, I spoke with him when he went to Manchester City. He is a big player for us.

“I do not know if I am the right man [to get the most out of Savio], but for sure he has to achieve. I think a player who is so good in one-on-one, so good at creating chances to score, to be complete, he has to score. If you analyse the other best wingers in the world, many of them, they score 10 to 15 goals per season. He has the qualities. Maybe his habits, he has to change habits, because he has to be focused on the assists, the one-on-one dribbling and also to score.”.

Omar Marmoush is closing in on an initial loan deal from Manchester City but that move is not complete and thus he is not available for Tottenham tonight. Micky van der Ven and Pedro Porro are both available having missed Tottenham’s loss at Brentford but the hosts are still without Xavi Simons, Pape Sarr, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert.

Charlton have made the perfect start to their Championship campaign; a 2-1 home win over Derby was followed up by a 2-1 victory at recently-relegated West Ham. Nathan Jones’ side earned their place in the League Cup second round with a 3-1 win at Cheltenham in the first round.

Recent findings suggest that “We have to be very organised and very professional, they [Tottenham] are a top team,” Jones said. “They have a great manager and a brilliant group of players. They already had a Premier League squad and they have spent, what is reaching about, I do not know, £300 million or something like that. It is a wonderful test, we have to be right near our best and do both sides of the game very well. Of course, you want to test yourself against the best managers and you want to test yourself against the best teams. For us, this is not our priority, the Championship is our priority, but this is the next game and therefore it is the most vital.”.

Additional major investment is expected towards the end of AMP8 and through AMP9. We continue to see strong growth in the U.K. water sector on the back of new projects and expanded frameworks as a part of this AMP cycle. Also in Water & Environmental, we have been awarded new work on BP's Hastings-on-Hudson site, addressing contamination in the surrounding uplands and the Hudson River. Our team is bringing together design, safety, schedule and cost planning to advance the site's long-term cleanup in a cost-effective way. Shifting to Life Sciences & Advanced Manufacturing, Jacobs was selected by Sanofi to serve as the EPCM partner for its new state-of-the-art insulin manufacturing plant in Frankfurt, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that the project will support production of multiple insulin products and strengthen supply reliability for patients around the world. Building on nearly 80 years of delivering the most innovative infrastructure to manufacture the world's most important therapies, this award reinforces our position as a leading provider of complex science-based solutions and reflects our ability to deliver large-scale, mission-critical investments from early project development through start-up. Finally, PA Consulting was selected as part of Sydney Airport's professional services framework, which is planning for future growth and increased passenger demand. The framework will support major programs that contribute to the airport's long-term development. This win reflects how we bring end-to-end capability to clients' challenges across the asset life cycle in the transportation sector.

According to recent reports, in summary, these awards help illustrate our differentiated and diversified model and underscore the growth opportunity ahead of us. Now I'll turn the call over to Venk to review our financial results in further detail.

Tackling The Trust Tax With Technology

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 30-year veteran in retail technology, Sensormatic Solutions President Tony D’Onofrio is leading the charge to redefine retail.
  • ​Amid economic pressure and supply chain volatility, prices can only be controlled to a point.
  • Sources indicate that retailers have embraced it, spending the past few years cutting friction from in-store operations at every turn and offering unstaffed checkouts and no-questions-asked returns in bids to win hearts when it matters most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 30-year veteran in retail technology, Sensormatic Solutions President Tony D’Onofrio is leading the charge to redefine retail.

​Amid economic pressure and supply chain volatility, prices can only be controlled to a point. Shipping delays and short staffing can still happen if a snowstorm moves through, no matter how meticulous the planning. But what happens on the floor? That’s something retailers can still control with relative confidence.​.

Sources indicate that retailers have embraced it, spending the past few years cutting friction from in-store operations at every turn and offering unstaffed checkouts and no-questions-asked returns in bids to win hearts when it matters most. Now, retailers are confronting the other side of the equation.​.

In a recent development, retailers’ investments in self-service touchpoints have yielded many of the customer experience benefits they promised. With shopper intentionality high and convenience still a top motivator, it’s no wonder self-checkouts (SCOs) are seen as a critical strategy for drawing in shoppers. Adjusted return policies have also become key, as nearly three-quarters (71%) of shoppers say they’re less likely to return to a retailer after a poor returns experience.​.

Industry observers note that however, other research highlights that these efforts to reduce friction at scale can come with unanticipated costs. It’s no surprise; as friction eases, retailers may unintentionally open the doors for exploitation. The expanded trust that must accompany self-service and relaxed policies has understandably been linked to increased losses primarily through increased crime activity.​.

And it’s true that stores offering SCO touchpoints see losses grow rapidly. Locations with SCO options see losses 33% higher than stores without them, on average, according to a recent ECR study. The study also found that grocery stores that implemented SCOs saw year-over-year losses increase by 22% in the first year of operations.​.

Further, every additional touchpoint can increase total losses across operations. Each transaction processed at an SCO carries a predictable and quantifiable loss. ECR found that a retailer’s total retail losses increase approximately 0.04% for every 1% of sales that occur at SCOs. This figure has quadrupled since 2018 (+0.01% for every 1%).​.

These patterns can be attributed, at least in part, to increased malicious behavior. A recent IHL Group study (conducted in partnership with my manufacturer, Sensormatic Solutions) found that theft remains the highest single driver of retail loss among respondents. However, the report notes that external theft—which includes any losses related to malicious customer actions—only accounts for 25% of all retail losses.​​.

Industry observers note that the ECR study offers some additional color. The study identified non-scans at SCOs as a factor in up to 4.8% of transactions, but it stops short of attributing intent with any certainty. The authors offer a range of 6% to 80%, which is to say that they can’t separate crimes from accidents with any confidence.​.

Of course, the trust tax reaches a peak around the holidays. More shoppers means more SCO use and more returns. A recent NRF report estimates that 15.8% of total annual sales end in returns; during the holiday period, this grows to 17% (download). As such, addressing the challenge and lowering the tax is at top of mind for retailers.​.

In a recent development, despite perceptions, retailers don’t have to decide between loss prevention and satisfaction. There’s a way to achieve the goal without touching the shopper experiences customers have come to expect. It starts with an adjustment to the leader’s understanding of the challenge at hand.​.

In a recent development, the source of the trust tax isn’t too much trust; it’s too little insight. Most shoppers can, in fact, be trusted. The concern is that, with traditional deterrents, a few bad actors—or a few mistakes—end in broad strategies that treat every shopper as suspicious. The result is additional punitive strategies, like bag checks and tightened return windows, placed in the wrong touchpoints and aimed at the wrong targets.​.

In a recent development, investments in item-level inventory monitoring tools can help balance the scales. As items move, exploitation leaves a fingerprint; unintended errors leave their own. Product journey records that integrate shipping, POS, exit and return data is where these markers appear, and they’re far more reliable than human surveillance or standardized checks.​.

Recent findings suggest that connecting these sources in real time can flag exceptions, such as an item leaving without a matching sale or a return without a matching purchase, so associates can act. They can also flag incidents at checkout that are more likely the result of error than theft.​.

Industry observers note that getting to this point requires retailers to lay a foundation. Using RFID tags and sensors, retailers can track items throughout their supply chains, storage facilities, sales floors and exits. This enables retailers to connect the dots between POS logs, exit data and returns to get a clear picture of loss within and beyond their walls.​.

Sources indicate that unified data can help retailers close that gap without touching the shopper—except in the places where increased friction serves them. These systems can surface mismatches in real time, so retailers can take steps to address what’s happening now and prevent it from happening later. This approach moves the friction from the shopper to the back end. The checkout and return stay as they are, while scrutiny goes to the exceptions the data flags.​.

A decade of self-service shopping has shown just how swiftly extending trust can become a cost center all its own. Addressing it ahead of the holiday rush has—for many retailers—meant deciding between satisfaction and shrink management.​.

Industry observers note that but data demonstrates that it doesn’t have to. The trust tax is predictable; it rises with use, peaks with traffic and starts as often with an honest mistake as with a bad actor. It’s in retailers’ own data that they’ll find solutions that enable them to address self-service losses without touching experiences. This holiday season, retailers who invest in insight won’t have to choose.

What Are Repositioning Cruises?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another.
  • Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.
  • It has been revealed that because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

It has been revealed that because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

Industry observers note that one key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

It has been revealed that repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

Industry observers note that if there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

Sources indicate that this journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

Industry observers note that if Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching Fresh York.

Growth continued to be driven by our position as the premium brand handset manufacturers, where we are adding device content and seeing steady design win activity with market leaders. SurgeSwitch extends our TVS content to higher voltage USB Power Delivery port now standard in smartphones and notebooks, maintaining consistent performance across temperature while conventional solutions derate. We view this as incremental higher value content for our mobile and computing customers with early adoption in industrial applications.

In a recent development, our PerSe capacitive sensor design win pipeline continued to expand across specific absorption rate, smart wearable and other consumer applications, and we are deepening engagement with our lead customers across a wide set of use cases. The combination of capacitive and force sensing, broadening our value to each customer strengthens retention and pull-through sensing and TVS content within the same accounts. As we highlighted at our Analyst Day, power-efficient analog connectivity is a critical enabler of the global AI build-out. Every generation of the compute demands more bandwidth at a lower power and a lower latency, and Semtech meets all this requirement with our high-speed analog solutions.

The market is moving toward us and Semtech is uniquely positioned to play a leading role in supporting this generational AI build-out. We are encouraged by our progress and also recognize that we are in the early innings and there is much work and execution on the horizon. I am convinced the best for Semtech is yet to come. With that, I will turn the call over to Mark for additional details on our financial results and our fourth quarter outlook. Mark?

Mark Lin: Thank you, Hong. For Q3, we recorded our 11th consecutive quarter of net sales growth with record net sales of $423 million, above the high end of the outlook range updated at our Analyst Day on October 15. Net sales grew 24% sequentially and 58% year-over-year. Net sales trends by end market, reportable segment and geographic region are included in the accompanying earnings presentation. Adjusted gross margin was 59.3%, up 480 basis points sequentially, up 630 basis points year-over-year and up 30 basis points from the midpoint outlook we provided at Analyst Day. Excluding the cellular module business, Q3 adjusted gross margin was 64.0%, consistent with the post-divestiture baseline we outlined at Analyst Day.

Adjusted net operating expenses were $111 million, 26% of net sales, improving from 30% in Q2 and improving from 32% a year ago, all while increasing R&D investment on key data center and LoRa programs and maintaining discipline in SG&A, which declined as a percentage of revenue, both sequentially and year-over-year. Our gross margin and operating expense profile flowed through to record adjusted operating income of $139 million and record adjusted operating margin of 33.0%, up 860 basis points sequentially and 1,240 basis points year-over-year. We also achieved record adjusted EBITDA of $146 million and record adjusted EBITDA margin of 34.5%, up 790 basis points sequentially and up 1,100 basis points year-over-year.

Semtech remained in a net interest income position for Q3. Our adjusted normalized income tax rate was 18%, consistent with our outlook. Adjusted diluted earnings per share was a record $1.17, above the high end of our updated guidance range from Analyst Day, up 65% sequentially and up 144% year-over-year. Operating cash flow for Q3 was $65 million, up 38% from $47 million a year ago and compares to $69 million in Q2. Q3 operating cash flow reflected investments in inventory and supply agreements to support projected business growth. Free cash flow for Q3 was $55 million, up 24% from $45 million a year ago.

Sources indicate that capEx was $10 million or approximately 2% of net sales and includes expenditures to grow our photonics capacity. Our Q3 ending cash and cash equivalents balance was $251 million and principal amount of debt was $503 million, resulting in net debt of $252 million and a net leverage ratio of 0.7x, down from 1.1x at the end of Q2 and consistent with our expectation we shared at Analyst Day of moving below 1x by the end of Q3. Now turning to our outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which is a 14-week fiscal period. We expect net sales of $480 million, plus or minus $5 million, up 13% sequentially and 75% year-over-year at the midpoint.

Recent findings suggest that our outlook includes the cellular module business for the full quarter, though we continue to expect to receive regulatory clearances and close the divestiture in Q4. A mid-quarter close would reduce cellular module revenue, but we expect it to increase adjusted operating margin with no meaningful impact on adjusted earnings per share. By end market, we expect an increase in infrastructure revenue led by data center. At our Analyst Day, we said we expected fiscal 2027 data center revenue would more than double from fiscal 2026. Our Q4 outlook now puts fiscal 2027 growth at more than 2.3x fiscal 2026, placing Q4 data center growth at about 40% sequentially and about 222% year-over-year.

This compares to Q3 year-over-year growth of 158%. We expect an increase in revenue from our industrial end market. LoRa is a second growth pillar for Semtech and grew 18% sequentially in Q3. For Q4, we expect LoRa to grow at a similar rate. We expect high-end consumer revenue to decrease about 10% sequentially, reflecting typical seasonal trends, partially offset by content gains in our TVS products. Based on expected product mix and net sales levels, we expect adjusted gross margin to be 58.9%, plus or minus 50 basis points. At the midpoint, this equates to a decrease of 40 basis points sequentially and an increase of 730 basis points year-over-year, reflecting the relative mix of lower-margin cellular modules revenue.

It has been revealed that excluding the cellular modules business, we expect adjusted gross margin of 64.3%, representing a 30 basis point sequential increase for this metric. Our gross margin outlook reflects the continued mix shift towards data center and LoRa, which carry gross margins that are among the highest in Semtech's portfolio, but also reflects incremental costs as we ramp capacity of our Photonics business. We expect gross margins to progress towards 70% in our Analyst Day model based on forecasted increases in 1.6T data center applications and growth in LoRa. Adjusted net operating expenses are expected to be $123 million, plus or minus $2 million.

Included in this outlook is increased R&D spend to accelerate time to market on key data center, photonics and LoRa projects, along with SG&A that continues to decline as a percentage of revenue. Our R&D investments continue to deliver strong returns and remain disciplined on SG&A. This results in an expectation of adjusted operating margin at the midpoint of 33.3%, up 30 basis points sequentially and up 1,510 basis points year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be $166 million, plus or minus $3 million, resulting in adjusted EBITDA margin at the midpoint of 34.7%, up 20 basis points sequentially and up 1,380 basis points year-over-year. We expect adjusted interest and other expense net to be approximately $0.5 million.

We expect an adjusted normalized income tax rate of 18%, unchanged from Q3 and reflecting expected geographic mix of income. These amounts are expected to result in adjusted diluted earnings per share of $1.33, plus or minus $0.03, up 14% sequentially and up 202% year-over-year at the midpoint. With that, I'll turn it back to Mitch.

Mitchell (Mitch) J. Haws: Thank you, Mark. We can now turn the call back over to the operator for the question-and-answer session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Quinn Bolton with Needham & Tech giant.

Quinn Bolton: Congratulations on the nice quarter and outlook. I guess I wanted to start with a question on the 14th week in the January quarter. Just what are you sort of assuming as part of the guide for that 14th week?

Mark Lin: Quinn, this is Mark. If I look through our portfolio of products, the 14th week, maybe if anything, it could benefit our consumer TVS business and the consumer business because we ship that business a little bit more linearly just from the volume of production. But we don't really look at the other businesses on a week-by-week basis. There's a little bit of batching for those products. But on OpEx, you [ did hit it ]. We would have about 7% incremental personnel expenses, but that's embedded in our forecast.

Quinn Bolton: Got it. Okay. So no real significant benefit on top line and probably an extra week on OpEx. And that's great. And then I guess, in the past, you've talked about having 50% or low 50% gross -- sorry, not gross market share estimate on 800-gig TIAs, and I think you've set a target to reach a similar market share on 1.6T TIAs by the end of calendar 2026. Just wondering if you feel like you're on track to hit that sort of 50% share target in 1.6T by the end of this year.

Hong Q. Hou: Yes. Quinn, thank you for the question. Yes. So for 800 gig, we come a long way from 2 years ago, 18% to now, we believe, well over 50%. And we have the same aspiration. We're seeing the same trajectory for 1.6T TIA. And remember, we come from early this fiscal year of 0 to now we are in the process of gaining share, and we have the same aspiration. And as we have the right product validated also by the industry award, we have the right capacity. We have the right engagement with the customers and 1.6T shipment is in the process of ramping up, and we do believe we'll get to that level in the near future.

Quinn Bolton: Is that -- do you think that's something you hit in fiscal '28 rather than, say, by the end of fiscal '27? Is that a more reasonable assumption to kind of get to those share aspirations?

In a recent development, hong Q. Hou: So when you see -- when you're in a steep ramp, it depends on which time line you would intercept, at which snapshot, at what time you're taking that. I do believe when we exit the year, we'll be having the market shares higher than today, and we'll continue that trajectory into the FY '28.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Timothy Arcuri with UBS.

It has been revealed that timothy Arcuri: Hong, you mentioned in the prepared remarks that supply, you said that it's kind of a driver for your optical business. Hong Q. Hou: Yes. Tim, that's a good question. So our supply is -- we have been working on the supply problem. About 2 years ago, we actually -- our operations team, especially our Chief Operating Officer, saw that, and we went out and qualified additional fabs and secure more capacity. At this point of time, the foundry capacity is not a limitation. And on the back end, we are building the diversification and also the resiliency as well. For example, some of the testers will have a longer lead time and -- but it's going to be supporting our FY '28 plan.

According to recent reports, so we view that as a differentiation because in the past, there are probably more competition and -- but now there are a few of us will have the capacity. And -- but this compounded with the growth -- with the performance and the qualification cycle since our product is already in the qualification with all module manufacturers, we know even for someone new to come in with a product, and they will have to go through the same process to get their customer and their customers qualified and even they have the security. So I'd say the combination of the performance, the road map alignment and secured capacity give us the confidence for the future growth trajectory.

Sources indicate that timothy Arcuri: Got it. And then, Mark, one for you. So gross margin is up like 30 bps on a pretty substantial sequential increase in some pretty high-margin businesses. So I would have thought maybe it could be up a smidge more than that. Can you just sort of talk, are there any cost like headwinds to that? And that's ex the module business, I mean?

According to recent reports, mark Lin: Yes, sure. Yes. So let's just say, 64% is not a holding point for us. So we expect growth in our gross margin, and we believe we have a clear path to our 70% gross margin target that we provided at Analyst Day. For Q4, there are a few moving pieces, some puts and takes, a little bit of mix, but there's also -- we're ramping the -- our photonics fab. So there's a bit of headwind there for the near term, but it's a pretty short near term. We project that, that business will -- that business ramp will come online and really contribute to our overall gross margins.

Now getting to that 70%, there's some pretty clear building blocks in my view, right? We're moving to 1.6T from 800 gig. That's kind of in the very near term. We have NPO that's additive to our gross margin. And then the market is moving towards a linear solutions, right? So just a lot more opportunity there to grow the business and grow gross margins.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Sean O'Loughlin with TD Cowen.

Sources indicate that sean O'Loughlin: Congrats on the results. So maybe dovetailing with Tim's last question, we've got data center -- in the guide specifically, we've got data center strong, LoRa strong. And I think that, that's about half of sales putting those 2 together. Maybe can you just talk about the puts and takes of that other bucket? I think you mentioned some memory supply constraints. And maybe just as a part of that, can you talk about the -- on the revenue side that's contemplated in the guide for the held-for-sale modules business?

According to recent reports, hong Q. Hou: Yes. So Sean, if I can address that question, you're right. There are some puts and takes. In general, the broad category of data center had higher gross margin. And if you double-click on that, the FiberEdge had a high gross margin accretive to the average margin. The fiber -- the CopperEdge even more so. There is a third piece of that growth pillar, the photonics. In Q4, we're projecting a meaningful contribution of the photonics. You know that the pretty latest business. We only became the product owner 9 months ago. So we are in a steep ramp in resources in development effort, in building up the infrastructure, in capital spending.

So that part of the contribution is a little bit of drag to the data center gross margin, but we are catching up very quickly. And among the portfolio, you're seeing puts and takes, that's the take. LoRa continued to be a very strong contributor in high margin and the rest of the portfolio is a balance. So 30 basis point sequential improvement, it's a meaningful step towards the 70% gross margin goal. We're pretty confident that the future growth driver gave us the opportunity to accelerate the gross margin improvement.

In a recent development, sean O'Loughlin: Great. And then as a follow-up, I just -- I wanted to ask about the second CopperEdge win that you mentioned, design win I guess, within the last 6 weeks. But then unless I misheard, a pretty short flash to bang for design win into actually shipping that to revenue. And I was just wondering if that -- maybe you could just talk about how that developed? And was the customer sort of waiting for the first design win to start shipping in volume, sort of see how it goes? Or if there was another dynamic that sort of is shortening the time line here?

Sources indicate that hong Q. Hou: Yes. Good question. So since the Analyst Day, it's only a few weeks. There seems to be a decade that's in development. There is good development in the CopperEdge front. There are 2 things. One is that with the existing customer, hyperscaler customer, we are in the process of ramping 1.6T ACC for backplane. With that customer, we secured 2 additional design wins of ACC for their new platforms. The second design win is, as we discussed, linear equalizer onboard, we have been actively engaging with multiple customers. We finally get one of them to the finish line and secured a design win of linear equalizer onboard for a major inference platform of that customer.

So we are projected to start ramping and shipping revenue in the first half of 2028 fiscal year.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Cody Grant Acree with StoneX.

Cody Grant Acree: Congrats on the progress. Maybe just following up on that last question. Hong, now with the expansion of your ACC design wins, your CopperEdge design wins, can you maybe talk about the breadth of your ACC engagements across hyperscalers and the various customer base? Can you talk about -- and also, are you any closer to helping us size the fiscal '28 CopperEdge opportunity and maybe even '28 or beyond?

According to recent reports, hong Q. Hou: Yes. So Cody, that's a good question. Thank you. So we have been talking about over the last 2 years, we spent a lot of effort evangelize the CopperEdge advantage in ACC for platform level and linear equalizer on board level. And we formed the ACC MSA and help to generate white papers and educate the entire industry. So the activity has been tremendous. And what we also found out that the ACC penetration at the cable level on platform just takes time. You need to find the right opportunity at the right timing for hyperscalers to redesign their platform, and that will be the right insertion point.

A couple of times with a possible proliferation where we found in the last month, they run out of time. So they will chose to use the existing solution. So pass now on the ACC at the backplane. But on the other hand, the linear equalizer onboard, the dynamics is very different. Hyperscalers redesigning the board, the compute board, the memory board and the switchboard almost on the monthly basis. What we found and when they found very often, they are shy in signal integrity from one end to other end for 200 gig.

And so traditionally, they have been using retimer type of simplify the DSP onboard, but we have been working and supporting the hyperscalers, some potential customers with our redriver solution, basically linear equalizer onboard. We still have to develop optionality for them to do AC coupling, DC coupling, number of channels, interchangeability, pin-to-pin compatibility with the retimers in case their qualification process goes sideways. So those are the time-consuming parts. The great news is that this hyperscaler, the second hyperscaler we were talking about and finished all of that and get the signal integrity on par or better than using retimer.

Industry observers note that of course, with the 90% of power saving with the removal of the latency and they chose to use a redriver instead of retimer to bridge the signal integrity. You can just imagine this is going to be a catalyst for other hyperscalers to use the same solution. And better yet, when the data rate goes to 400-gig per second, you -- the signal can now even travel from one side of the board to the other side of the board without a retimer or redriver. So you're going to see for 400-gig per lane, the linear equalizer onboard is going to become a mainstream solution. So we are very excited about this.

Cody Grant Acree: Maybe moving to NPO, CPO. Can you maybe help to give us some color on the shape of the ramp that you expect next year, specifically at NPO? And how are those engagements transitioning to design wins? And how does your dollar content at TIAs and drivers compared to your module dollar content?

Sources indicate that hong Q. Hou: Yes. Good question, Cody. For CPO, we are developing CPO scale-up lasers, but that's a contribution of potential revenue beyond 2027. On the other hand, NPO, we do believe by the second half of 2027, we have a meaningful revenue contribution. To us, as I mentioned that before, NPO is LPO on steroid. They use the same content of linear equalizer -- linear TIA, linear drivers. And also, we have our VHP lasers can be incorporated with 8-lane or 4-lane silicon photonics modulator to make the laser in the module, in the optical engine.

So our content compared to pluggable transceivers is going to grow from just the TIA to TIA-plus driver for at least and then with the potential to insert lasers. We talked about we are in development for photodiode, high-speed photodiode, but that's probably too late to insert into the 1.6T or 3.2T NPO at 200-gig per lane, and we are preparing for future product. So NPO, we are very well positioned. CPO is a story for 2028 and beyond, and we'll see the meaningful revenue in the second half of FY '28.

Cody Grant Acree: Hong, any help on the content increase of adding the driver and the lasers versus just the TIAs?

Sources indicate that hong Q. Hou: Yes. So we talked about that before for linearized application, DSP-less applications, the requirement is more stringent. Therefore, there is incremental premium for the product.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Joe Moore with Morgan Stanley.

Joseph (Joe) Lawrence Moore: I wonder how you think big picture about potential problems with land, power, shell in data centers, given that it could be a constraint on your business, but also a lot of the drivers of using your products are sort of getting to a lower power budget, lower power footprint within the rack. How are you thinking about that dynamic as we look forward?

Hong Q. Hou: Yes, Joe, so for data centers, certainly, the powers are used to support the infrastructure. But even for the key pillars between compute, memory and networking, a majority of the power are consumed in the compute complex. For networking, people report anywhere from 15% to 20% of total power consumption. They absolutely favors the low-power solutions. So the linear solution -- linear analog solution typically save power from 90% to 50%. That is why people are moving from pluggable optics to NPO and better yet CPO in the future to even reduce the power consumption in the first couple of centimeters.

So I think that's why in our prepared remarks, we think the market is moving toward us and the industry and networking architecture increasingly favors low-power linear analog solutions, and we are going to be riding on that trend.

In a recent development, joseph (Joe) Lawrence Moore: Great. And then separately, there's been news about potential restrictions on Chinese transceiver models. And given the breadth of your business, can you just talk about any impact that you may have from that?

Industry observers note that hong Q. Hou: Yes. So we are paying a close attention to that. But the good news is that all the major module manufacturers are our customers. If that were to happen, there would be some shift between the different customers and shipment between the different customers. So it wouldn't be any meaningful impact to us. So we are the pure-play component supplier and many of the U.S.-based customers are our largest -- among our largest customers.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Rick Schafer with Oppenheimer.

Sources indicate that richard (Rick) Ewing Schafer: I'll add my congratulations, guys. You've kind of hinted at it a couple of times, Hong. You've mentioned HieFo. And I was kind of looking for a little bit more of an upgrade there. I know you guys are clearly investing in capacity. I know you talked, I think, in the past about potentially quadrupling capacity by the end of this year and then doing the same next year. So I was curious if you could level set us on sort of where capacity will be in units, revenues exiting next year in terms of your laser capacity? And any sense of design win or revenue funnel tied to that?

And I'm curious, part of my question is, too, is that all like 250-milliwatt lasers? Or does that include some of the new high-power 400-milliwatt stuff? And if I could sneak in just the last little thing. I think Mark mentioned, if I heard them correctly, that lasers and PDs are actually going to be gross margin accretive as they ramp. So I just wanted to make sure I heard that correctly.

Hong Q. Hou: Yes. So Rick, let me address your questions. So HieFo product is built upon this pretty differentiated high wall plug efficiency laser platform. So right now, we are supplying in volume, the gain chips using tunable lasers to support metro and scale across data center applications. The same design, but with the cavity coated delivers a narrow linewidth and low noise and high power efficiency attributes. So those are ideal characteristic for coherent-lite. So we are sampling multiple customers for coherent-lite optical transceiver applications. For that, typically, they only need about 100 to 150 milliwatts, and our laser can do that day in, day out.

Then I talked about the VHP lasers for IMDD intensity-modulated direct drive, which can be incorporated in 1.6T optical transceivers. And really, we are targeting to get them insert into 3.2T optical transceivers in future years because our laser can deliver 250-milliwatt single-mode power with excellent beam profile, it allows a very low loss coupling into silicon photonics modulator and waveguides. So we are engaging with several customers in applications and it can be as early as 1.6T to insert. Then, of course, we use that platform to deliver -- to develop ultra-high power lasers for CPO scale up for future years.

So we have multiple drivers and they're coming on to the market at a different time in future years and the road map of alignment and customer engagement activities are really quite exciting. Right now, we are gated by the capacity. So that's why we're increasing capacity, and we're on track, as I noted, to expand the capacity by 3 to 4x by the end of this year and another 3 to 4x by the end of next year. By 3x increase, for example, end of this year, we will be having the capacity to support a run rate of $25 million a quarter. And of course, you can just scale that by the future capacity increase.

Mark Lin: And Rick, you heard us right. We expect the Photonics gross margins to mirror data center gross margins.

Richard (Rick) Ewing Schafer: And then just hopefully a quick one, but I'm just curious, on ACC and linear equalizer onboard, clearly, that's an emergent market. It seems to be, especially on the board level at the board side, it seems like it's happening quicker than I expected. I can speak for myself. I guess as we look forward, I mean, how do you look at that combined TAM between ACC like the cables and then the onboard, the linear equalizer application. So if you're splitting that market or however you want to talk about it, Hong, but I'm curious, I mean, is this roughly a balanced market? Or do you see onboard being a much bigger opportunity?

Hong Q. Hou: Yes. So Rick, these are all emerging opportunities, and I think it's hard to quantify, but I would imagine the linear equalizer onboard easier to apply and is a bigger market opportunity than the ACC for backplane interconnect.

As you talk to your customers or your hyperscaler, I guess, friends in the valley, what are you hearing in terms of the outlook and the conversations you're having for demand for 2028 calendar?

Recent findings suggest that hong Q. Hou: Yes. So Harsh, I can answer that question. Yes, you were saying that compare notes with my peers, I probably have more opportunity to do that recently because I often get calls from my customers to pull in the demand and escalate and they want to get more parts sooner well within the lead time. And across the board, the demand here and especially for us is very robust. We have the record booking in Q3 and record backlog. And also, as we discussed, the future architecture is to our favor, linear analog applications to save power for high data rate, low latency and low power consumption and also the customer engagement activities on multiple programs.

We talked about FiberEdge for 1.6T, NPO, CPO, linear equalizer onboard, ACC, photonics for transceivers and photonics for coherent-lite and photonics for scale across tunable lasers and future CPO scale-up lasers. The activities and opportunity is just enormous. So I do -- that's why -- that's what gives me the confidence and the conviction for 2028 calendar year. We, at Analyst Day saying that FY '27 to '26, we're going to be double -- more than double the data center revenue. Well, now if we take the midpoint of the guidance, FY '27, we'll be finishing the data center with revenue roughly about $520 million. That represent about 133% year-over-year growth.

We are pretty confident based on these 3 factors I just talked about the backlog, the industry trend and the momentum, we're going to be double that in FY '28 to over $1 billion.

In a recent development, tore Egil Svanberg: Hong, Mark, Mitch, congratulations on a record quarter. So Hong, there's been a lot of macro things happening since your Analyst Day. I mean I assume it's a scale thing because obviously, you have to offset some fixed costs, right? But any guidepost on that scale or anything like that, that you could share with us would be really helpful.

And I think the rest of the portfolio, 1.6T, both in FiberEdge and CopperEdge will help propel gross margins. Like we said before, 64% is not a holding point, right? We expect some meaningful growth off of that 64% base.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Craig Andrew Ellis with B. Riley Securities.

Craig Andrew Ellis: Congratulations and congrats on getting ACC -- equalizer-enabled ACC really going at the number of hyperscalers. I wanted to follow up on the comment that we expect initial NPO revenue in fiscal 2 half '28. And it seems like we're engaged with both hyperscalers and module makers. Can you talk a little bit more about the breadth of engagement on both of those sides? And would you expect revenues to ramp from both types of customers or primarily one of the 2?

Hong Q. Hou: Yes. So we got -- Craig, a pretty broad engagement with pretty much all of the major module manufacturers and the hyperscaler -- on the hyperscaler side, probably about 4 in the U.S. and 3 in China. Those are the major hyperscalers. They are having very active NPO programs. And -- but of course, they usually are having multiple module suppliers engaged in supporting their pursuit. So we're seeing pretty diverse form factor in terms of the densities and number of lanes, and we're doing some customization in order to fit into their form factor. But some of them are pretty close and pretty far along.

Arsenal will host old nemesis José Mourinho’s Real Madrid in the league phase of the Champions League.

Mourinho, the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur manager, will return to London to resume hostilities against last season’s beaten finalists.

Other reunions from Thursday’s draw include Manchester City travelling to Barcelona, to whom they last week sold Rodri, and Liverpool visiting Inter Milan, who have signed Curtis Jones.

In a recent development, arsenal will also travel to Harry Kane’s Bayern Munich, while United will host the Germans as well on their Champions League return in a repeat of the legendary 1999 final. Michael Carrick’s side will also visit Cesc Fàbregas’s Como.

Mourinho last managed at the Emirates Stadium in March 2021, barely a month before his sacking by Spurs.

During his two spells as Chelsea manager, Mourinho famously had run-ins with Arsenal’s Arsène Wenger.

Mourinho called Wenger a “specialist in failure” after the Frenchman failed to add to his three Premier League titles following his Portuguese counterpart’s arrival in London in 2004.

Last season, Mikel Arteta finally ended Arsenal’s long wait to be crowned champions of England but agonisingly missed out on European glory.

Recent findings suggest that verdict Premier League champions should not be daunted by any game, but Real Madrid – with Mourinho in control – has the feel of a defining match of the group stage. Facing Kane in Munich does not seem any easier. Some tough assignments here including a trip to Napoli but the pot-four teams seem straightforward for Mikel Arteta.

Sources indicate that verdict Playing against the European champions and travelling to Barcelona will be a true test of how much progress Enzo Maresca has made in the short time he has been at the Etihad Stadium. City’s other games do not look easy either but they should be defeating teams such as Sporting Lisbon and Porto – at least they would be expected to under Pep Guardiola.

In a recent development, verdict The San Siro was where Arne Slot began to turn results around last season and Iraola getting a win there would be a massive statement. Atlético staged a comeback at Anfield in 2020 and the repeat fixture will be tight. But there are enough winnable games there for Liverpool to reach the next round.

Verdict They will face a wall of noise in Istanbul when they play Galatasaray, but Villa will look to get points from the game. There are some tasty destinations for travelling fans and getting results there will ease the pressure on the match against PSG, who have been rattled by Villa before but remain a difficult opponent. The Nou Camp is a place where momentum can change in a season – for good or bad.

Verdict The repeat of the 1999 final is the standout fixture, but Michael Carrick should be looking beyond that match for the points needed to progress. He has been given a tough set of away games to navigate. They are winnable but difficult. So those games at Old Trafford will be very crucial.

That brings our coverage of the Champions League draw to an end, as the 36 teams found which eight teams they will be facing in the league phase of this season’s tournament. Thanks for joining us!

The league phase will kick off on 8 September and will be wrapped up after all teams play at the same time on 27 January.

The top eight teams of the league phase progress to the last 16 automatically, while teams that finish between ninth and 24th will be forced to navigate a play-off tie to reach the knockout stages.

So we have 144 fixtures decided but there are certainly a few heavyweight contests which stand out:.
